q: In 2023, which new name replaced NAFLD?
a: SLD (steatotic liver disease, the umbrella term)
exp: A 2023 multi-society Delphi consensus renamed NAFLD to MASLD to emphasise metabolic dysfunction.

q: What is the new umbrella term for all liver disease with >5% hepatic fat?
exp: SLD (steatotic liver disease) is the umbrella term covering MASLD, MetALD and ALD.

q: What was one reason for retiring the name NAFLD?
a: It could not be separated from alcohol-related liver disease
The name could not be used in children
exp: The exclusionary "non-alcoholic" label and the stigma of "fatty" prompted a name that reflects the pathophysiology.

q: What does MASH describe?
a: A subtype of MASLD with inflammation
exp: MASH adds inflammation and hepatocyte injury to fat and carries a higher risk of progressing to fibrosis.

q: MASH can be diagnosed even at F0. What defines 'at-risk MASH'?
a: MASH with fibrosis stage F2 or higher
ALT more than twice the upper limit
exp: MASH with fibrosis stage F2 or higher has clearly higher liver-event and mortality risk, so it is classed as at-risk MASH.

q: Why is MASLD commonly underdiagnosed?
a: It is symptomless and liver enzymes are often normal
Ultrasound cannot detect it in most patients
Only a liver biopsy can establish the diagnosis
It is rare in people under 50 years of age
exp: Most patients have no symptoms and often normal liver enzymes, so it is found incidentally.

q: Compared with the general population, overall mortality in MASLD is:
exp: All-cause mortality in MASLD is about twice that of the general population and rises with fibrosis, not fat.

q: Which factor most strongly drives prognosis in MASLD?
a: The amount of liver fat (steatosis grade)
exp: Prognosis is set by the fibrosis stage, not by the amount of fat.

q: On average, MASH fibrosis progresses by one stage every:
exp: MASH fibrosis advances about one stage every 7 years, accelerating to about 2 years from F3 to cirrhosis.

q: What is the initial non-invasive index for fibrosis screening in primary care?
exp: FIB-4 is calculated from age, AST, ALT and platelets, making it a first-line screen usable in primary care.

q: What is the FIB-4 low-risk cutoff for ages 35-65?
exp: At ages 35–65 a FIB-4 below 1.3 is low risk and rules out advanced fibrosis.

q: If FIB-4 is 1.3 or higher, what comes next?
a: An ELF blood test or transient elastography (VCTE)
exp: A FIB-4 of 1.3 or more leads to a second step: an ELF blood test or transient elastography (VCTE).

q: What does VCTE (transient elastography) measure?
exp: VCTE measures liver stiffness in kPa as a gauge of fibrosis.

q: AASLD recommends MASLD screening in which patients?
a: People with type 2 diabetes or obesity
Every adult at a health check-up
Only people with raised liver enzymes
exp: People with type 2 diabetes or obesity have a high MASLD prevalence and are the screening targets.

q: A 5-7% weight loss is expected to bring:
exp: Liver inflammation starts to improve with a 5–7% weight loss.

q: A 7-10% weight loss can additionally bring:
exp: With a 7–10% loss, fibrosis can improve as well.

q: Which diet has the strongest evidence in MASLD?
exp: The Mediterranean diet has the strongest evidence for reducing liver fat, even independent of weight loss.

q: An exercise prescription that improved MASLD parameters was:
a: 40-minute aerobic or resistance sessions three times a week
One two-hour high-intensity session a week
Start exercise only after weight loss
exp: Three 40-minute aerobic or resistance sessions a week improve liver fat and ALT within 12 weeks.

q: Which blood biomarker helps overcome underreported alcohol intake?
exp: PEth reflects alcohol intake over the past 1–4 weeks and complements self-report.

q: In MASLD, even low-level alcohol intake is:
a: Even that may harm the liver
Up to one drink a day protects the liver
Wine is an exception and is safe
Men can safely have two drinks a day
exp: Even low alcohol intake can harm the liver in MASLD, so restraint is advised.

q: In fibrosis staging, what does F4 mean?
exp: F0 is normal, F1–F3 progressive fibrosis and F4 cirrhosis.

q: What does MetALD describe?
a: Steatosis with alcohol intake above the MASLD limit
Steatosis from alcohol alone without metabolic risk factors
MASLD with two or more metabolic risk factors
exp: MetALD is steatosis with metabolic risk factors plus alcohol intake above the MASLD limit.

q: What is the female alcohol threshold within the MASLD definition?
a: Under about 1.5 drinks (20 g) a day
Under about 2 drinks (30 g) a day
Under about 1 drink (10 g) a day
exp: MASLD allows under 20 g a day (about 1.5 drinks) for women and under 30 g for men.

q: Which item is NOT part of the FIB-4 formula?
exp: FIB-4 uses age, AST, ALT and platelets; blood pressure is not part of it.

q: What is the FIB-4 low-risk cutoff for patients 65 or older?
exp: Because age is in the formula, the low-risk cut-off is raised to below 2.0 at 65 and older.

q: VCTE readings can be unreliable in patients with:
a: Severe obesity, ascites or heart failure
The fasting state before the scan
exp: VCTE can be unreliable in severe obesity, ascites or heart failure.

q: The CAP score from VCTE reflects:
exp: CAP reflects liver fat, while LSM reflects fibrosis.

q: FIB-4 of 1.3 or more plus liver stiffness above 8 kPa calls for:
a: Recheck in primary care after six months
exp: A FIB-4 of 1.3 or more with stiffness above 8 kPa warrants referral to hepatology.

q: Progression from F3 fibrosis to cirrhosis takes on average:
exp: From F3 to cirrhosis takes about 2 years on average, much faster than the early stages.

q: The intensive lifestyle trial that improved MASLD prescribed:
a: A 750 kcal daily deficit plus 200 minutes of walking a week
A 300 kcal daily deficit plus 60 minutes of walking a week
A 1,500 kcal daily deficit plus an hour of running every day
No calorie limit, 150 minutes of walking a week
exp: A 750 kcal daily deficit plus 200 minutes of walking a week that achieved 5–10% loss improved inflammation and fibrosis.

q: Which brief alcohol screening tool is used in primary care?
exp: AUDIT-C is a simple three-item alcohol screening tool.

q: In the Mediterranean diet, what should be kept low?
exp: The Mediterranean diet cuts processed meat and added sugar while adding vegetables, whole grains, olive oil and fish.

q: Which Korean-language name did KASL adopt for MASLD?
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — nomenclature
exp: KASL adopted 대사이상지방간질환 as the official Korean name for MASLD.

q: What are the KASL 2025 diagnostic criteria for MASLD?
a: Hepatic steatosis on imaging or biopsy plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor and no significant alcohol intake
Hepatic steatosis plus at least two cardiometabolic risk factors is required
A liver biopsy confirming steatohepatitis is mandatory for diagnosis
Hepatic steatosis plus a BMI of 25 or higher is required
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — definition
exp: MASLD is diagnosed by hepatic fat plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor and no significant alcohol intake.

q: Which waist-circumference cut-offs did KASL adopt as the cardiometabolic criterion for Koreans?
a: ≥90 cm in men, ≥85 cm in women
≥94 cm in men, ≥80 cm in women
≥102 cm in men, ≥88 cm in women
≥90 cm in men, ≥80 cm in women
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — Korean waist cut-offs
exp: Given average Korean waist sizes, the domestic cut-offs are 90 cm for men and 85 cm for women.

q: What BMI threshold defines overweight/obesity as a cardiometabolic criterion for Asians in MASLD?
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — Asian BMI cut-off
exp: For Asians a BMI of 23 or more counts as a cardiometabolic risk factor.

q: What is the daily alcohol limit allowed within the MASLD definition?
a: Under 30 g in men and 20 g in women
Under 20 g in men and 10 g in women
Under 40 g in men and 30 g in women
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — alcohol threshold
exp: Under 30 g a day for men and 20 g for women is the alcohol limit allowed in MASLD.

q: How closely does the MASLD-defined population overlap with the former NAFLD population?
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — >95% concordance with NAFLD
exp: The MASLD population overlaps the former NAFLD population by more than 95%, so earlier evidence still applies.

q: Roughly how common is MASLD among Korean adults?
a: About one in three or four adults, more often in men
About one in twenty adults, similar in both sexes
About one in ten adults, more often in women
More than one in two adults, similar in both sexes
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — Korean prevalence 27.5–33.5% (men > women)
exp: Korean studies put MASLD prevalence at 27–34%, one in three or four adults, more often men.

q: What does the guideline identify as the leading cause of death in MASLD?
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — prognosis
exp: The leading cause of death in MASLD is cardiovascular disease rather than liver disease.

q: Which MASLD patients should undergo hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance?
a: Those with confirmed or suspected cirrhosis
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — HCC ≥1.5%/yr in cirrhosis
exp: With cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma develops at 1.5% or more per year, so surveillance is recommended.

q: Per the KDA fatty liver statistics, what share of adults with type 2 diabetes had fatty liver (FLI ≥60)?
src: KDA Fatty Liver & Diabetes Statistics in Korea (2009–2017) — 29.6% in 2017
exp: One in three adults with type 2 diabetes has fatty liver by a fatty liver index of 60 or more.

q: Among young adults (20–39) with type 2 diabetes, what share had fatty liver (FLI ≥60) in 2017?
src: KDA Fatty Liver & Diabetes Statistics in Korea (2009–2017) — ages 20–39: 42.2%→60.1%
exp: Among young adults with type 2 diabetes, fatty liver rose from 42% in 2009 to 60% in 2017.

q: What is specifically emphasised when diagnosing MASLD in children and adolescents?
a: Other causes of hepatic fat (such as inborn errors of metabolism) must also be reviewed
A liver biopsy is mandatory to confirm the diagnosis, unlike in adults
A BMI cut-off of 30 is applied instead of the adult criteria
Only the alcohol history needs checking; no further review
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — paediatrics
exp: In children, other causes of hepatic fat such as inborn errors of metabolism must also be reviewed.

q: Which factors does the guideline name as raising extrahepatic cancer risk in MASLD?
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline — extrahepatic cancer risk
exp: Obesity and type 2 diabetes are the main factors raising extrahepatic cancer risk in MASLD.

q: Which first-line imaging test is most commonly used to detect fatty liver?
exp: Abdominal ultrasound is the most common first-line imaging test for fatty liver.

q: Which of the following is NOT a cardiometabolic risk factor used to diagnose MASLD?
exp: The five cardiometabolic factors are weight/waist, glucose, blood pressure, triglycerides and HDL; smoking is not one.

q: What is the foundation of treatment for MASLD?
a: Lifestyle change for weight loss: diet and exercise
exp: Lifestyle change for weight loss through diet and exercise is the foundation of MASLD treatment.

q: Which index is used first to gauge fibrosis risk in a person with diabetes and fatty liver?
a: FIB-4 (from age, AST, ALT and platelets)
exp: FIB-4, from age, AST, ALT and platelets, is the first index used to gauge fibrosis risk.

q: Why does abdominal (visceral) fat matter in fatty liver?
a: Fatty acids released from visceral fat flow through the portal vein straight into the liver
A larger waist shrinks the liver
exp: Fatty acids from visceral fat reach the liver directly through the portal vein and drive steatosis.

q: What most strongly determines prognosis in MASLD?
a: The amount of fat in the liver
exp: The fibrosis stage determines prognosis in MASLD.

q: How is fatty liver usually discovered?
a: Incidentally, on tests done for another reason, because it causes no symptoms
src: Glen J et al. BMJ 2016 (NICE NAFLD guideline) (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: Fatty liver rarely causes symptoms, so it is usually an incidental finding on tests done for other reasons.

q: What is the most common blood-test pattern in fatty liver?
src: EASL–EASD–EASO Clinical Practice Guidelines. J Hepatol 2016 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: ALT higher than AST is the most common blood-test pattern in fatty liver.

q: On average, how long does simple fatty liver without inflammation or fibrosis take to reach cirrhosis?
src: Glen J et al. BMJ 2016 (NICE NAFLD guideline) (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: Simple steatosis without inflammation or fibrosis progresses slowly, about 57 years to cirrhosis, but far faster once inflammation appears.

q: Which test gives the definitive diagnosis of liver fat, inflammation and fibrosis?
src: EASL–EASD–EASO Clinical Practice Guidelines. J Hepatol 2016 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: Liver biopsy is the reference test that confirms fat, inflammation and fibrosis.
